note.body:
How do we get there? The way we always have, by letting go. This is 2026. Back we go.
(press)
2011. A school in a slum.
(press)
I was the teacher, the owner, the coach. I did everything in that school.
(press)
Then two hundred schools in our name. We chose the teachers and wrote the curriculum, and our coaches were there. What we gave away was running the school.
(press)
Then government schools. The government's teachers, the government's curriculum. All we held was our coaches.
(press)
Then Tanzania, Moawin and Rawalpindi, and we gave up our own coaches too. We recruited others to do the work with us. That was much harder. We committed to it, because this only works as a movement, not one organisation doing it itself.
(press)
And now people do not even need us. ScienceFuse took our code to build a science teaching assistant. A developer in Niger runs it for their school, without ever asking us. A team in Germany took it to offer to their own government.
[Haroon, in your own words, only what you know first-hand: 7ate9 and Africa. From your brief: "7ate9, and how they cloned our repo" (facts2 found no source for the Gates contracts, so they stay off the screen.)]
(press)
People said we would lose out, that we would run out of money.
(press)
This year we closed the largest grant in our history. Funders who said no to us three times have come back.
[Haroon, in your own words: the Nina Jean story. From your brief: "one of them has even sort of blocked us" Say "eleven years" and "now funding us" only if you are sure.]
Letting go and recruiting others is harder, and it brings more success and more scale.
(press)
note.first_line: How do we get there?

cues: press 1: page 2: two ways of counting cost, direct and all-in
press 2: moves to a21
note.body:
If someone asks how we got twelfth. The table divides how much more children learn by what it costs. If Rawalpindi moves children as much as similar programmes do, about 0.2 of a standard deviation in a year, at about three dollars a child, that is about eight per hundred dollars: twelfth on the table, with Malawi's programme counted.
(press)
Two honest limits. Nobody has measured Rawalpindi's effect yet, and three dollars is the direct cost. If we count every cost, as the leadership team agreed, and use Islamabad's figures, we sit between thirty-third and fifty-sixth. The table's dollars are 2015's, so the comparison is on the cautious side. To reach twenty at three dollars, children's learning has to more than double.
(press)
note.first_line: If someone asks how we got twelfth.

scenes.title: Above 20: the three that train no teachers

cues: press 1: page 2: Malawi's maths programme, about 20 per $100, Prevail's verified figure
press 2: moves to a22
note.body:
If someone asks about the programmes at the very top. Three score above twenty, and none of them trains teachers. In Madagascar, families were told what schooling earns. In Indonesia, schools were linked to village councils. In Kenya, children were grouped by level. That is why we say first among programmes that improve learning through teachers. Of those, the best today are community preschools in Mozambique, about sixteen, and Argentina, about fifteen. Twenty passes both.
(press)
If someone asks about Malawi's maths programme. About twenty per hundred dollars is Prevail's verified figure, shared with us in October. The published table has no row for it. Worked out on the table's own scale from the trial, it reads about four, which is why you may see two numbers. We use Prevail's.
(press)
note.first_line: If someone asks about the programmes at the very top.

cues: press 1: page 2: by the one move (group work, different levels, better questions)
press 2: moves to a23
note.body:
If someone asks how we know. We took 907 debriefs in Islamabad and compared each teacher's next lesson with one before, on the skill they were coached on. We matched them with 1,271 similar teachers who recorded on the same days and had no debrief. Twelve in a hundred moved up a level, against ten. A small gain, and a real one: before any debrief there was no such change.
(press)
By the one move: group work and teaching to different levels moved; asking better questions, the most common topic, did not. That split was not in our written plan, so it is a strong lead, not yet a finding. One catch: fewer debriefed teachers recorded again within four weeks, 73 in 100 against 83, so we keep checking.
(press)
note.first_line: If someone asks how we know.

scenes.title: Practice alone: what the data holds

cues: press 1: page 2: how far to trust it
press 2: moves to a24
note.body:
If someone asks how we counted the practice at the end of a lesson. Islamabad, August to October, 7,412 lessons teachers recorded, each checked step by step against its plan. In about one in three, the children never practised on their own. In about one in seven, they did all of it. With a coach in the room it happens a little more: 28 in 100 coach visits skipped it, against 33 in 100 of teachers' own recordings.
(press)
How far to trust it. The checking is done by an AI on the audio, so it is ours, not an official figure. We left out lessons that were not the lesson on the plan. A second count, one week in September, came out the same: about a third skipped, about one in seven did it all. An early-stopped recording looks the same as a skipped step. Our coaches' read is that time runs out; teachers rarely refuse the plan.
(press)
note.first_line: If someone asks how we counted the practice at the end of a lesson.

cues: press 1: moves to a25

If someone asks who uses our open code. A science education group, ScienceFuse, took it to build a science teaching assistant, and they are setting it up now. Someone in Niger runs it for their schools, without ever asking us. A team in Germany took it to offer to their own government. There were nineteen public copies on GitHub this morning, and a copy need not show up there, so there may be more.
[Haroon, in your own words, only what you know first-hand: 7ate9. facts2 found no source for it, so it is not on the page.]
